new.title: The First Adolescent Super-Earth-Sized Multi-Planet System Around an M Dwarf: TOI-2079
new.summary: We identify two planets in close-in orbits around the M-type star TOI-2079 as the first super-Earth-sized planets orbiting a multi-planet M dwarf with a well-determined age of $1$-$2$\,Gyr. The interior planet, TOI-2079 b, has an orbital period of $1.49232359^{+0.00000099}_{-0.00000086}$ d, and the outer planet, TOI-2079 c, has an orbital period of $9.3174523\pm0.0000098$ d. The host star characterization is based on spectroscopic observations, which classify it from an M1.5 to an M3.5 dwarf with an effective temperature of $3695\pm77$ K. Further analysis determined TOI-2079's rotation period to be $17.33^{+0.29}_{-0.28}$ d. Multiple ground-based follow-up observations, combined with a state-of-the-art validation procedure, allow us to rule out possible astrophysical false-positive scenarios and validate the planetary nature of both objects. We find that the inner planet has a radius of $1.320\pm0.050 R_{\oplus}$ and $T_{\rm eq} = 867\pm27$ K, while the outer planet has $R_{\rm p} = 1.671\pm0.051 R_{\oplus}$ and $T_{\rm eq} = 473\pm15$ K.

new.title: Modelling scintillation in Fast Radio Bursts
new.summary:
Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are bright, ms-duration, extragalactic radio transients. Propagation through inhomogeneities in the ionised medium produces scintillation, observed as frequency-dependent intensity variations in their spectra, with bright patches, called scintles. The characteristic scintillation bandwidth probes scattering material along the line of sight. Measuring this scale can be challenging when the observing bandwidth of the burst spectra contains a few scintles. We study the uncertainties associated with recovering $
u_s$ from frequency autocorrelation functions (ACFs) under finite-bandwidth conditions. We examine the recovery of $
u_s$ from individual ACFs and investigate if averaging multiple independent ACFs provides a more robust measurement. Using simulations, we reproduce observational conditions to investigate the modelling of scintillation in ACFs and the associated measurement uncertainties. We use these simulations to test the finite scintle error (FSE) prescription and assess its applicability to real observations. We test the resulting modelling framework on Effelsberg Ultra Broad Band receiver observations of the repeating FRB 20240114A. As the number of scintles decreases, individual ACFs develop fluctuations that deviate from the expected Lorentzian profile. This results in increased scatter in the recovered $
u_s$ and a less reliable FSE prescription. Averaging multiple independent ACFs mitigates these effects and improves the recovery of $
u_s$ in the low-scintle regime. Our results provide a framework for ACF modelling and uncertainty estimation in FRBs. For individual bursts, the FSE is effective with sufficient scintles; we find $\eta = 0.055$ more suitable for FRB analysis and update the FSE accordingly. For repeaters, averaging multiple ACFs and bootstrap resampling improve the recovery and uncertainty estimation of $
u_s$.

new.title: Blowing star formation away in AGN Hosts (BAH) - VI. Warm Molecular Outflows Driven by the Low-Luminosity AGN in NGC 3884
new.summary: We use the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) Medium Resolution Spectrograph (MRS) to investigate the warm molecular and low ionization gas outflows driven by the low-luminosity Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) in NGC 3884. By decomposing the emission-line profiles into multiple Gaussian components, we detect both ionized and warm molecular outflows, traced by [Ar ii] 6.99 um and H2 0-0 S(5), respectively. The ionized and warm molecular components both extend to similar distances from the nucleus, reaching approximately ~1.2 kpc. In addition to an outflow component, we detect a double narrow emission component in both ionized and molecular lines, clearly observed along the minor axis with similar amplitudes, while their intensity ratio varies systematically along the major axis. Both components exhibit similar line widths and centroid velocity distributions, indicating that they are not associated with outflows, but instead arise from gas in the galaxy disk. We estimate that the outflow injects momentum into the interstellar medium (ISM) at a rate corresponding to ~0.015 percent of the AGN bolometric luminosity, consistent with a radiation-driven origin. Assuming a constant outflow rate, the gas reservoir would be depleted on a timescale of ~26 Myr, potentially suppressing nuclear star formation in the host galaxy.

new.title: WISDOM Project -- XXIX. Catalogue of CO observations of nearby galaxies and the CO Tully-Fisher relation
new.summary: We present Tully-Fisher relations (TFRs) that use carbon monoxide (CO) as the kinematic tracer and Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) $W1$-band and Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) $K_\text{s}$-band magnitudes as tracers of stellar luminosity. CO data were obtained using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array for the mm-Wave Interferometric Survey of Dark Object Masses (WISDOM) project for a sample of $102$ galaxies located at redshifts $z \lesssim 0.03$, with $81$ detections. The best-fitting reverse $W1$-band and $K_\text{s}$-band CO TFRs are $M_{W1}=(-7.18\pm0.93)\left[\log\left(\frac{W_{50}/\sin i}{\text{km~s}^{-1}}\right)-2.6\right]+(-24.04\pm0.13)$ and $M_{K_\text{s}}=(-5.95\pm0.62)\left[\log\left(\frac{W_{50}/\sin i}{\text{km~s}^{-1}}\right)-2.6\right]+(-24.01\pm0.10)$, respectively, where $W_{50}$ is the velocity width of each integrated CO spectrum at $50\%$ of its maximum, $i$ is the galaxy inclination and $M$ is the galaxy absolute magnitude. Our results are in excellent agreement with those of Tiley et al. (2016b), and together they constitute a robust local benchmark for the CO TFR. We however measure a shallower slope and a smaller zero-point offset compared to the relation of Tully & Pierce (2000). Due to the morphological diversity of our sample, we construct separate late-type and early-type galaxy (ETG) CO TFRs, finding that ETGs are $1.40\pm0.39$~mag fainter at $W1$ band and $0.89\pm0.28$~mag fainter at $K_\text{s}$ band at a given velocity width. We also generate and include a comprehensive catalogue of WISDOM CO data products for use in future molecular gas studies.

new.title: The GAPS programme at TNG. LXXXIII. Orbital refinement and atmospheric investigation of TOI-1518 b (BD+66 1610 b)
new.summary: TOI-1518 b (BD+66 1610 b) is a highly irradiated ultra-hot Jupiter on a strongly misaligned orbit, a benchmark target for atmospheric and dynamical studies. We comprehensively characterise the TOI-1518 system by refining its orbital and physical parameters, and by investigating the chemical composition of the planetary atmosphere through transmission spectroscopy. We employed a joint Bayesian framework combining TESS photometry, HARPS-N high-resolution spectroscopy, and least-squares deconvolution profiles to break stellar geometrical degeneracies. We then applied single-line and cross-correlation function (CCF) transmission spectroscopy across theoretical templates. By anchoring the stellar projected rotational velocity ($v \sin i_\star \approx 79.7$ km s$^{-1}$), we confirmed the nearly polar orbit ($\lambda \approx 238^\circ$) and the theoretically predicted nodal precession ($\mathrm{d}i/\mathrm{d}t \approx 0.15^\circ$ yr$^{-1}$). We revealed an atmospheric Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) effect and a bulk atmospheric blue-shift of $\approx -7.0$ km s$^{-1}$. Through transmission spectroscopy, we detected H I, C I, Na I, Ca I, Sc II, Ti II, V II, Cr I, Fe I, Fe II, Ni I, Sr II, Y II, Eu II, and W I. This marks the first detection of H I, C I, Sc II, V II, Sr II, Y II, Eu II, and W I in this planet, and the first ever detection of Eu II and W I in an exoplanetary atmosphere. Inconsistencies in the Na I doublet shifts suggest likely stellar contamination. Furthermore, time-resolved CCF analysis revealed morning-to-evening limb asymmetries for species like Mg I and Ba I, hinting at night-side cold traps. The atmosphere of TOI-1518 b exhibits a rich chemical inventory shaped by intense irradiation and bulk circulation. Our results emphasize the necessity of simultaneously modelling stellar line morphology and planetary tracks to accurately interpret atmospheric signals under strong RM effects.

new.title: Hints of planet formation in progress around DR Tau from observations with LBT SHARK-NIR and SHARK-VIS
new.summary: Protoplanetary disks are the primary sites of planet formation. However, the direct imaging of protoplanets still embedded within their parental disks remains a significant challenge, with only a small number of confirmed detections to date and several candidates awaiting verification. We search for embedded planets in the protoplanetary disk of the young star DRTau by targeting accretion signatures from forming sub-stellar objects. Using narrow-band imaging, we observe both visible Halpha and near-infrared Paschen-beta (Pabeta) emission to identify actively accreting companions. To this end, we performed high-contrast observations of DRTau using the SHARK-VIS (0.40-0.95 micron) and SHARK-NIR (0.96-1.70 micron) imagers at the LBT. The study uses a combination of narrow-band filters to isolate accretion signatures and broad-band filters for multi-wavelength characterization in both the visible and near-infrared. Our observations recover the primary disk structures previously identified in the literature, albeit at low signal-to-noise (S/N). We identify two compact features with S/N between 6 and 13 in both narrow- and broad-band filters. The first, an elongated structure, matches previous SPHERE detections, while the second, more compact feature, is now confirmed despite its low S/N in earlier datasets. A comparison over a seven-year baseline confirms the stability of both structures. Their observed orbital motion is consistent with Keplerian rotation, potentially suggesting the presence of an undetected planetary-mass companion (few MJup) at the location of the second feature. However, our analysis does not confirm Halpha or Pabeta emission originating from localized accretion. Instead, we conclude that the observed flux is likely stellar light reflected by dust at these locations and discuss alternative mechanisms that could account for such detections.

new.title: PHOTO-CAT - Photometric Contamination Analyzer Tool: A High-Performance Framework for Photometric Contamination Assessment
new.summary: High-precision photometric missions are sensitive to flux contamination from neighboring stars, which can bias light curves, dilute transit depths, and compromise photometric precision. We present PHOTO-CAT, a catalog-driven, mission-agnostic tool for quantifying stellar flux contamination in photometric observations. The tool builds a three-dimensional Euclidean representation of the sky from a user-provided astrometric catalog, indexes it with a memory-optimized KDTree for rapid neighbor searches, and computes per-target contamination metrics from angular separation, relative fluxes, and configurable aperture models (top-hat or circular Gaussian PSF), optionally converted into an arbitrary instrumental bandpass via empirical photometric relations or stellar spectral models. A streaming, CSR-style storage format with compact internal identifiers enables scalable processing of catalogs with tens to hundreds of millions of sources with minimal memory overhead. Outputs include per-target contaminating flux, contamination ratios, target purity, number of neighboring sources, and their angular separations, supporting target screening and field-selection decisions ahead of observations. We demonstrate the software performance on all-sky Gaia samples (G <= 12, with neighbors down to G = 17; over three million targets), providing global contamination statistics and spatial characterization of crowded regions, and apply it to the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample to show how wavelength-dependent contamination estimates support target selection and observing-geometry optimization. Although developed for the Mauve satellite, PHOTO-CAT is mission-agnostic and readily applicable to TESS, PLATO, Ariel, and other surveys.

new.title: Characterisation of B-type stars in four young Galactic open clusters. II. Photometric variability with TESS and identification of pulsating stars
new.summary: Pulsations and binarity are important properties of massive stars and influence their structure and evolution. Young open clusters are ideal laboratories to study massive stars, since they are mostly coeval and chemically homogeneous. We analyse 82 B-type stars in the Galactic open clusters $h$ and $\chi$ Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, and NGC 1960, which have ages between 15 and 30 Myr. We extract light curves using both simple aperture photometry and a point-spread-function-based method that minimises contamination from crowded fields in full-frame images from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. We successfully extract light curves for 63 stars. The majority have photometric variability caused by pulsations, showing how pulsations are a common property of young B-type stars in clusters. We classify stars into different pulsator types based on their spectral type and frequency spectrum. The most common pulsator class are beta Cephei stars, with 29 stars in total, and we discover pulsation modes in almost all stars with a spectral type of B2 or earlier. All Be stars show pulsations, which supports the consensus of the ubiquity of pulsations in these stars. Finally, we confirm that the majority of early B-type stars are in binary systems, except for two pulsating Be stars and a star with rotational modulation. This indicates that pulsations do not significantly bias the spectroscopic detection of short-period binaries, except for Be stars where the spectroscopic radial velocity variability threshold should be higher than the typical value of 20 km s$^{-1}$.

new.title: Probing for relativistic outflows in the Ultraluminous X-ray pulsar RX J0209.6-7427
new.summary: Context. Relativistic winds have been observed in Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), but their detection at large distances remains limited. Galactic neutron stars accreting matter from Be-star companions provide a valuable opportunity to improve our understanding of these outflows. Aims. RX J0209.6-7427 is a Be-XRB, powered by a neutron star with a spin period of 9.3 seconds, that underwent an outburst in 2019, exceeding a bolometric luminosity of $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at its peak. Owing to its relatively low distance and a high-resolution XMM-Newton observation, this source is a strong candidate for investigating outflows associated with super-Eddington accretion. Methods. The RGS spectrum yields 105,000 counts, a factor of two higher than any other deep ULX RGS spectrum. RGS and EPIC-pn data sets were modelled with a phenomenological continuum accounting for emission from the accretion disc and accretion column. The emission and absorption features were fitted with the optically-thin plasma models available in SPEX, exploring the temperature-velocity parameter space. Results. The modelling of emission features suggests the presence of a multiphase photoionised plasma approximately at rest with respect to the source. The absorption features can be reproduced either by blueshifted photoionised absorbers moving at approximately $0.1c$ and $0.2c$, the latter being more tentative, or by an alternative collisionally ionised absorption model, which provides a comparably acceptable fit. The presence of ultrafast outflows therefore remains a plausible, but non-unique, interpretation of the data. If associated with outflows, the inferred column densities appear lower than those reported for some persistent ULXs, potentially reflecting differences in the accretion-flow properties or the shorter super-Eddington phase of RX J0209.6-7427.

new.title: Disrupted stars and captured compact objects: Combining observations from multiple messengers to infer the population of massive black holes
new.summary: Massive black holes (MBHs) are found in galactic centres, but their formation and evolution remain elusive. Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) both arise from stellar dynamics in the nuclear star clusters around MBHs, and are observed with electromagnetic surveys and gravitational waves, respectively. To overcome the scarcity of coincident detections, we formulate how to combine gravitational-wave detections from LISA-EMRIs with observations from ZTF-TDEs to measure properties of the MBH population. Building on two-dimensional Fokker-Planck simulations of EMRIs and TDEs, we model how their populations are affected by the MBH-host scaling relation, the nucleation fraction and the MBH occupation fraction, and analyse the resulting catalogues using joint hierarchical inference accounting for their individual selection biases. With current ZTF-TDE detections, we can already identify combinations of MBH formation favoured by and consistent with the observed TDE population, and derive corresponding predictions for the EMRI population detectable by LISA. Across a range of astrophysical assumptions, the ratio of detectable TDEs to EMRIs is high: ZTF detecting 2.7-84.3 times as many TDEs as LISA detects EMRIs. TDEs, through their numbers, set the shared mass and redshift distributions: LSST constrains the characteristic MBH mass to a 90% credible width of 0.31 dex and the power-law index of the redshift evolution to a precision of 0.11. EMRIs make up ~3.4% of the joint catalogue, yet carry more information than the whole ZTF sample and are the only probe of MBH spin and orbital eccentricity. TDEs will constrain the abundance of low-mass MBHs before LISA flies, while EMRIs will measure properties that electromagnetic surveys cannot. EMRI and TDE observations offer complementary insights into MBH growth and evolution that neither can provide alone.

new.title: The Time Domain Telescope: A Global Spectroscopic Array
new.summary: The Time Domain Telescope (TDT) is an initiative in the context of the ESO Expanding Horizons program. The TDT project aims for a global telescope array for spectroscopic time-resolved and time-critical observations in the optical-near-infrared, with a core at the European Southern Observatory and partners around the world. The TDT core consists of 100 unit telescopes of 2-meter diameter each that are fully Adaptive Optics-assisted in the blue, to deliver an enclosed energy of >=80% within 0.12" at 400nm. The unit telescopes are coupled to a set of spectrographs covering spectral resolutions R=10^3 - 10^5 over the wavelength range 0.35 - 1.8 micrometer. The combination of extreme adaptive optics with near-read-noise-free detectors will allow the TDT to reach unprecedented depths and/or high cadence. When all 100 units target a single object a depth of 25 mag can be reached in 30 minutes at a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 per spectral resolution element at a spectral resolution of R=5000. With this the TDT will spectroscopically match the imaging depth of the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Euclid and Roman spacecrafts, the expected brightness of electromagnetic counterparts discovered by the LISA space mission, as well as by the next-generation gravitational wave detectors. The science of the TDT covers a large part of astronomy, and ranges from the outer Solar System, to stellar and binary systems to extragalactic transients and the growth of supermassive black holes, all the way back to the expansion history of the Universe. The TDT is transformational, unique and highly complementary to the current and near-future ESO facilities, in particular by providing the possibility for time-resolved spectroscopic observations well below the brightness of the optical night sky.

new.title: TDI-$\infty$ and beyond
new.summary: Time-delay interferometry (TDI) cancels the laser frequency noise that dominates the measurements of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), and relies on interpolating the laser noise to fractional delays. In TDI-$\infty$, which finds the laser noise free combinations from a linear model of the measurements, the interpolation sets the design matrix, and any interpolation error leaves uncanceled laser noise which is not accounted for. We introduce Gaussian process (GP) interpolation into TDI-$\infty$, which models the laser noise from its spectrum and propagates its interpolation error into the likelihood as a covariance. We test it on a realistic data model in which the measurements pass through the on-board anti-alias filter and are downsampled to the 4 Hz telemetry rate, either applying the filter after the delays, as on the spacecraft, or building the filter into the GP kernel. We compare it with Lagrange and cosine-sum interpolation, and also keep the column space of the design matrix, which the standard null space likelihood discards. In lisainstrument simulations all three interpolators cancel the laser noise for a 1 Hz filter band edge, but only the GP does so up to the 2 Hz Nyquist frequency, a range the Lagrange and cosine-sum interpolators were not designed for. In parameter estimation on 200 simulated galactic binaries, the GP with the filter in its kernel gives the smallest calibrated posteriors. The differences are small for a single long data segment and grow when the data are split into short chunks or contain gaps, where the column space also recovers some information, by an amount that depends on the threshold that defines the null space.

new.title: 2026 QQ8: Earth's temporary flyby of maximum lunation
new.summary: Aims: On a rare occasion, asteroids are temporarily captured by the Earth to become the planet's interim companions. The discovery of asteroid 2026~QQ$_8$ provided an opportunity to study this class of objects, adding to the sparse discovery catalogue of Earth's temporary companions. Methods: We performed astrometric, photometric, and dynamical studies of 2026~QQ$_8$, and measured its solar radiation pressure signal to discern between a natural and an artificial origin. Results: We find 2026 QQ$_8$ to be of natural origin, with solar radiation pressure signal commensurable with natural objects and spectrophotometry of an S-type object. 2026 QQ$_8$ is Earth's third discovered otemporarily-captured companion on a flyby orbit, and the first long-duration one, owing this to being on the so-called "orbit of maximum lunation". Its unusual orbit lies close to the theoretical upper duration limit of an object captured in the Earth-Moon system, and has now been observed for the first time.

new.title: Precise Interstellar Extinction Estimates for Nearly Ten Million Stars Based on Multiple Spectroscopic Surveys
new.summary: Accurate interstellar extinction estimates are vital for revealing the intrinsic physical properties of stars and the dynamic structure of the Milky Way. Based on multiple optical and near-infrared spectroscopic surveys, including LAMOST, APOGEE, GALAH, GaiaESO, SEGUE, and DESI, we use MLPs and polynomial regressions to calibrate giants and dwarfs separately onto the APOGEE parameter scale, constructing a combined spectroscopic catalog of nearly ten million stars with calibrated stellar atmospheric parameters. This catalog not only provides a robust dataset for our extinction measurements, but also serves as a reference sample for estimating stellar parameters from photometric surveys. Both cross-survey comparisons and external comparisons with high-resolution spectroscopic benchmarks show good agreement in the calibrated parameters. By applying the star-pair method to this extensive sample, we obtain precise extinction estimates. Incorporating distance information, we characterize the spatial distribution of extinction covering over 33,000 square degrees of the sky. Comparisons with existing literature demonstrate that our extinction estimates achieve an exceptional precision of 0.019-0.022 mag. The value-added catalog and open-source Python pipeline for line-of-sight extinction released in this work will provide robust support for future Galactic structure studies and photometric calibrations.

new.title: What determines the properties of Population III binaries?
new.summary: Population~III binaries may provide a gravitational-wave probe of the first stellar populations. Uncertain initial binary parameter distributions and evolutionary prescriptions complicate predictions of their remnant masses, birth orbits and formation spins. Varying these model evolutionary parameters (MEPs) jointly is needed to identify which MEPs shape each property and whether their effects persist among binaries that merge. We use \textsc{StarTrack} to evolve $2\times10^6$ initial binaries per model across 1152 configurations spanning eight MEPs. To our knowledge, this is the largest grid of Population~III isolated-binary population-synthesis models to date by number of distinct parameter configurations. We compare the properties and correlations of all binary black holes (BBHs) with those of systems that merge within the adopted age of the Universe. The all-BBH (merging-BBH) model medians span $34.3$--$171.0 M_{\odot}$ ($23.1$--$94.8 M_{\odot}$) in total mass, $0.039$--$0.106$ ($0.018$--$0.129$) in effective aligned spin $\chi_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at formation, and $0.075$--$0.639$ ($0.039$--$0.983$) in birth eccentricity. Merger selection also changes correlations between BBH properties and the combinations of MEP values and prescriptions associated with them. We use variance-based sensitivity analysis to quantify how the initial binary parameter distributions and evolutionary prescriptions affect the predicted BBH properties.

new.title: Carving the Neptunian desert as a function of stellar mass and lifetime XUV irradiation
new.summary: The Neptunian desert is a prominent feature in the exoplanet population, thought to arise from both XUV-driven photoevaporation and tidal circularisation following high-eccentricity migration. However, the extent to which each mechanism contributes, and where, remains uncertain. We examine the desert as a function of stellar type as a test of these mechanisms. We determine the desert boundaries for subsamples of F, G, K, and M-hosted planets for radius against period, semi-major axis, bolometric instellation, and lifetime XUV irradiation. Going from F to M, we observe shifts in the boundary between 2.2-7.5 R$_\oplus$ towards shorter orbital periods, smaller orbital distances, and much smaller instellations. These shifts match changes in lifetime XUV irradiation as a function of stellar mass at fixed period, semi-major axis, and bolometric instellation, evidence towards a photoevaporative origin for the desert at these radii. This is especially the case for orbital period, where the boundary should be invariant across stellar types under the high-eccentricity mechanism. In lifetime XUV space, we see significant overlap in the boundary across stellar types up to 7.5 R$_\oplus$. While this could be further evidence towards the XUV-driven mechanism in this regime, our uncertainties cannot rule out a shift in the boundary of the magnitude expected under the high-eccentricity mechanism. Overall, our results suggest a photoevaporative origin of the Neptunian desert up to sub-Saturn radii, but increased sample sizes, especially for M-hosted, Neptune-sized planets, will help distinguish further between the mechanisms.

new.title: Hotter than Little Red Dots: Two Quasars with $T\sim10^4\,\mathrm{K}$ blackbody-like continua at $z\sim4$
new.summary: Gas envelope models of Little Red Dots (LRDs) predict a transition from cool ($T\sim5000\,\mathrm{K}$), gas-enshrouded accretion to an exposed quasar, but observational candidates remain scarce. We identify two blackbody quasars (BBQs), JADES1180 at $z=3.711$ and GTO1215 at $z=4.552$, among 3,553 sources with archival NIRSpec/PRISM spectra. Both show extremely red rest-frame UV ($\beta_\mathrm{UV}>2.0$) but blue optical continua ($\beta_\mathrm{opt}<-0.75$), where $f_\lambda\propto\lambda^\beta$. Their $\Lambda$-shaped UV-optical continua peak at $\lambda\approx3000-4000$ Å and are not reproduced by a quasar template reddened with an SMC-like extinction curve. Under the gas envelope interpretation, UV-to-mid-infrared spectral energy distribution fitting indicates $T_\mathrm{env}\approx7600-10300\,\mathrm{K}$ and $L_\mathrm{env}\simeq(3-15)\times10^{45}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, placing both sources just above the typical LRD ranges in temperature and luminosity. Both BBQs show hot-dust emission with $T_\mathrm{dust}\simeq1400-1550\,\mathrm{K}$ and X-ray emission with $L_\mathrm{2-10\,keV}\simeq(1.3-4.5)\times10^{44}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. The gas absorption is $N_\mathrm{H}<1.5\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$, indicating Compton-thin absorption sightlines. Both also exhibit far-infrared and millimeter detections, suggesting an additional cooler dust component, potentially associated with their host galaxies. These properties are consistent with a transitional phase in which a hotter gaseous envelope partially exposes the central engine.

new.title: A TESS Search for Optical Variability in Intermediate-mass Black Hole Candidates
new.summary: Optical variability of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) probes accretion onto black holes. We study the optical variability of AGNs in the mass range of intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, $10^{2-6}\,M_\odot$), whose expected variability damping timescales are of order days. We use the high-cadence photometry of the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) to search for optical variability within its individual 28-day sectors. By applying the Quaver light-curve reduction pipeline and designing artifact-aware variability metrics, we identify 3 sources with high-confidence variability and 17 sources with medium-confidence variability. Fitting damped random walk (DRW) models reveals a tentative timescale-mass correlation in a small, metric-selected subset, but not in the full sample. ZTF difference-image aperture photometry reveals long-term fractional variability of 1.8-7.4% in the high-confidence sources, while most medium-confidence sources have variability below 1%. This study demonstrates that the dense cadence and repeated full-sky observations of TESS are valuable for detecting IMBH optical variability, while also being limited by its instrumental artifacts and relatively shallow field.

new.title: An early interaction between the Sagittarius dwarf and the Milky Way I: Fossil signatures in the phase-space structure of the disc
new.summary: Several independent lines of evidence point to an early encounter between the Milky Way and the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy $5$-$7$ Gyr ago. We present four controlled $N$-body+hydro simulations, one of an isolated host galaxy and three of a single interaction between a Milky-Way-like host and a Sagittarius-like satellite on an unbound polar orbit. Relative to the fiducial satellite (with total mass $0.7\times10^{11}$ M$_\odot$), one run increases the satellite's mass by a factor of $1.5$ and another its crossing speed by a factor of $1.4$, giving pericentric speeds of $466$-$634$ km s$^{-1}$ at pericentric radii of $R\simeq15$-$18$ kpc. Comparing the present-day, phase-space structure in radial bins by age of newly-formed thin-disc stars across the runs, we find that stars that existed at the time of the passage are thickened by up to $\sim37$ per cent in mass-enclosed height and heated by up to $\sim5$ km s$^{-1}$ in vertical velocity dispersion relative to the control, while stars formed after the passage are unaffected. The heating signature is also evident when comparing the age-vertical velocity dispersion relation against a heating relation with a power law of $0.38$, obtained by fitting the isolated host. A single, disc crossing from an early interaction thus suffices to leave lasting, datable fossils in the age-resolved vertical structure of a galactic disc. The fiducial run's dispersion jump of $\sim4$ km s$^{-1}$ matches best with that observed in the outer low-$\alpha$ disc of the Milky Way (Das et al. 2024), corresponding to a perturber mass of $0.7\times10^{11}$ M$_\odot$, with a velocity of $466$ km s$^{-1}$ at a pericentric radius of $16.7$ kpc, though the inversion from jump amplitude to perturber mass is good only to a factor of $\sim1.5$.

new.title: Atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances of young stars with APOGEE -- II. Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, and Sulphur abundances in Orion
new.summary: We derived the abundances of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, and iron in young G-, K-, and M-type stars (effective temperatures of 3500--5900 K) using APOGEE-2 infrared spectra. Our final sample comprises 195 slow rotators ($v\sin i$ $\leq$ 30 km~s$^{-1}$) in the Orion complex (Orion A, B, OB1, and $\lambda$~Ori). The abundances were determined using MARCS model atmospheres, atmospheric parameters derived with \tona, and the \bacc\ code. We obtained median abundances of $\epsilon$(C) = 8.37$\pm$0.10, $\epsilon$(N) = 7.35$\pm$0.16, $\epsilon$(O) = 8.63$\pm$0.08, $\epsilon$(S) = 7.19$\pm$0.18, and $\epsilon$(Fe) = 7.45$\pm$0.05. Nitrogen is subsolar ([N/H] $=-0.48$), whereas carbon, oxygen, sulphur, and iron are within 0.1 dex of the solar values. We find no spatial structure within the Orion subgroups, and the only significant difference is a 0.29 dex lower nitrogen abundance in Orion A than in Orion OB1, which does not extend to the other elements. Compared with 430 nearby main-sequence stars analysed in the same way, Orion shows carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances lower by 0.1--0.2 dex, although consistent within the errors, whereas sulphur and iron differ by less than 0.07 dex. We also compare our abundances with nebular abundances of HII regions and star-forming galaxies: the stellar abundances of oxygen, sulphur, and iron are higher, with the largest offset in iron, although the agreement in abundance ratios improves when temperature inhomogeneities and dust depletion are taken into account.

new.title: Recovering buoyancy-glitch parameters in low-luminosity red giants from global stellar properties with machine learning
new.summary: Buoyancy glitches in red giants provide localized information on the interior structure near the base of the convective envelope, but their properties are typically inferred from dedicated seismic modelling rather than global properties, limiting large-sample applications. We investigate whether the buoyancy-glitch amplitude ($A_g$), location ($W_{\rm g}^{\star}$), and width ($D_g$) can be recovered from global stellar properties using gradient-boosted tree regressors (XGBoost and LightGBM). The models were trained on a grid of 12580 synthetic stellar models of low-luminosity red giants, with target parameters derived from fits to the local buoyancy frequency profile. We find that $W_{\rm g}^{\star}$ and $D_g$ exhibit excellent recoverability, achieving test-set $\mathcal{R}^2$ values of 0.98 and 0.97, respectively. In contrast, $A_g$ shows moderate recoverability overall ($\mathcal{R}^2=0.68$). This reduced recoverability of $A_g$ is concentrated in the large frequency separation range $\Delta\nu = 4.6$--$18.9\,\mu$Hz, where the glitch resides in the evanescent-zone transition between the convective envelope and the gravity-mode cavity, increasing intrinsic scatter. SHAP analysis shows that $\nu_{\rm max}$ and $T_{\rm eff}$ dominate the predictions across all targets, indicating that the regressors rely primarily on evolutionary state. While $W_{\rm g}^{\star}$ and $D_g$ are tightly constrained by global evolutionary trends, the lower recoverability of $A_g$ reflects localized structural complexity associated with red-giant evolution. Overall, for the synthetic grid adopted here, these results indicate that global properties provide a direct estimate of the buoyancy-glitch parameters and a way to prioritise dedicated mixed-mode inversions for large asteroseismic samples such as Kepler and PLATO.

new.title: Nearly pristine gas and hard ionizing radiation one billion years after the Big Bang
new.summary: The first stars formed out of light elements (H, He, and Li leftover from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis) and began the chemical enrichment of the Universe. Identifying this first-generation population of stars, known as Population III, and understanding their properties is one of the most ambitious goals of modern extragalactic astrophysics. We report the detection of He and H emission lines and extremely low Oxygen abundance in AMORE6, a strongly magnified galaxy at redshift z = 5.725, i.e. approximately one billion years after the Big Bang, with deep James Webb Space Telescope spectroscopy. He II lambda1640 and lambda4686 emission lines are detected at 16.7 sigma and 4.0 sigma significance, respectively. The observed He II-to-Hbeta ratios are consistent with predictions for extreme ionizing radiation fields and the low chemical compositions typical of Population III stars. Oxygen abundance of the interstellar medium is estimated to be 8 x 10^-4 solar from weak [OIII]lambda4363 and lambda5008 lines, consistent with an almost pristine environment, perhaps enriched by the Pop III stars themselves. Although we cannot exclude alternative sources of hard ionizing radiation, such as accreting black holes, these observations offer the first view of the extremely low metallicity environment where the Universe's first stars are predicted to be born. The data show that such pockets of pristine gas still exist one billion years after the Big Bang and that they are dominated by very massive stars.

cross.title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
cross.summary: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.

cross.title: Dark Energy Based on Modified Gravity: Where the Future Lies?
cross.summary: Based on current observational data, there is a strong possibility that dark energy was in a phantom regime in the near past, and a transition from a phantom to a quintessential regime may have occurred. Since then, many scenarios compatible with the DESI data have been proposed. In particular, there exist several realistic models in the framework of $F(R)$ gravity. In this paper, we show that such realistic models of $F(R)$ gravity may produce an anti-gravity or ghost graviton in the future. The problem could be avoided by further changing the parameters and fine-tuning the initial conditions, but we propose to introduce a potential barrier of the scalar field for the small scalar curvature region, which prevents the Universe from evolving into the anti-gravity or having a ghost graviton region, without the fine-tuning of the initial conditions. We also discuss how this regime can be tested using peculiar velocity and kSZ effect probes.

cross.title: A Relativistic Newton's Third Law for Binaries in Environments
cross.summary: We derive the relativistic form of Newton's Third Law governing the interaction between intermediate- and extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and surrounding relativistic matter fields. Working within a two-parameter expansion, we rewrite the evolution of the secondary's orbital elements in a form resembling the integrated forces acting on the environment, avoiding the need to calculate any gravitational perturbations sourced by the dynamical matter content. Using the retarded and advanced Green's functions, we obtain both instantaneous and orbit-averaged laws relating the rate of change of the secondary's orbital energy and angular momentum to that of the matter and the gravitational-wave fluxes at that order. Our results clarify and correct the mixture of ad hoc balance prescriptions currently employed in the literature, providing first-principles forcing functions for the secondary's orbital elements in two ready-to-use forms: a leading-order formulation suitable for fast evaluation with complex relativistic matter simulations, and a first-post-adiabatic formulation of the energy and angular-momentum evolution in environments that are stationary and axisymmetric at leading order.

cross.title: Cosmological Correlators with Triple Massive Exchanges
cross.summary: Among all tree-level contributions to the primordial bispectrum, the triple exchange of massive scalars is the most challenging. In this paper we present an analytical formula for this bispectrum in the form of a double series, which allows the three exchanged fields to have different masses and converges throughout the whole physical region. We obtain it by expanding the mixed propagator with the softest momentum, so that the triple exchange becomes a sum of integrals over two mixed propagators. Each of these integrals satisfies a differential equation and is fixed by its value at equal momentum. We further show that the squeezed limit follows directly from this formula and takes a simple and compact form.

cross.title: Nuclear Urca cooling in magnetar crust and anomalous heating
cross.summary: We present a new result that the nuclear Urca process in magnetars, associated with ultrastrong magnetic field, dramatically alters the neutrino cooling efficiency to support higher surface temper ature, which is not common in ordinary neutron stars. A new formalism for neutrino luminosity accommodating finite temperature on top of magnetic field is extended with the use of realistic nuclear structure inputs for the Urca pair 29Na-29Mg. We find that the neutrino luminosity of Urca pair shows a spiral variation as a function of magnetic field and crust density, while the Urca pair persists, in contrast to previous studies. Applying geometrically correct volumetric energy loss rate to Urca shell at fixed density with varying magnetic field strength, our results show that thermally populated excited states at finite temperature enhance neutrino luminosity, whereas conditions con strained Urca-pair formation driven by ultrastrong magnetic field reduce cooling efficiency, which can explain high temperature of magnetar surface as a new possibility.

cross.title: Coronagraphic time-delay interferometry: fundamental steps towards concrete applications
cross.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is a future space-based gravitational wave (GW) observatory. Central to LISA data analysis is time-delay interferometry (TDI), which reduces otherwise overwhelming laser frequency noise. In previous work, we explored coronagraphic TDI, a sky-dependent null-stream channel which cancels the GW signal of a point-like source when pointed at its sky position. Because this property relies only on the geometric response of LISA, coronagraphic TDI is a candidate for model-agnostic sky localization. Here, we address three challenges which arise when analyzing realistic LISA data: (i) spacecraft motion; (ii) signal superposition; (iii) instrumental noise. We derive a second-generation coronagraphic TDI variable and its analytic noise model, and show that it reduces laser frequency noise in the presence of spacecraft motion while still recovering the position of the source. Using pairs of Galactic binaries (GBs), we find that sources can be localized independently provided they do not overlap in frequency, even when they share the same sky position, whereas sources overlapping in frequency can only be localized if one dominates by a factor of ~100 in amplitude. This is confirmed by the analysis of a simulation containing a massive black hole binary and 49 verification GBs. Finally, we introduce a statistical test based on the analytic noise model, which provides well-calibrated confidence regions for the sky position of the source. Applying it to GBs in the presence of instrumental noise, we find that the geometric response alone only weakly constrains the sky position: even at signal-to-noise ratios of order 10^4, 90% confidence regions span ~10^3 deg^2. These are fundamental steps towards applications of coronagraphic TDI to LISA data, such as sky localization and glitch discrimination, which we discuss.

cross.title: Nuclear Precision and Multimessenger Constraints on Neutron-Star Structure
cross.summary: Neutron-star cores retain structural freedom beyond the constraints supplied by nuclear measurements. We quantify this freedom through an observable-dependent variance ceiling and identify radius--Love compensation as a mechanism suppressing nuclear constraints on tides. Across four data-conditioned equation-of-state families, a pulsar radius measured to 0.3 km paired with a binary tide measured to 10\% removes 44--68\% of the current logarithmic Love-number variance. The framework connects laboratory precision and complementary stellar measurements to core structure.

cross.title: Diffusing the assumptions: towards realistic LISA stochastic component separation with physics-aware simulation-based inference
cross.summary: Simultaneous global-fit inference of the numerous sources observed by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) depends on accurate modeling of its stochastic components: instrumental noise, the Galactic foreground, and astrophysical or stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds (SGWB). Realistic features such as non-Gaussian transients and data gaps challenge traditional likelihood-based pipelines, creating an opportunity for simulation-based inference (SBI) to augment traditional analyses. Here, we present an SBI framework for LISA stochastic component separation built on the Simformer, a transformer trained with diffusion or flow matching that ingests the full time-delay interferometry cross-spectral matrix via a physics-aware embedding. We progressively relax standard simplifying assumptions on simulated 11.6-day datasets containing a loud foreground and a faint power-law SGWB. With unequal arms and per-link noise freedom, the networks match 17-dimensional MCMC posteriors after importance reweighting; full cross-spectra constrain each link's optical metrology noise amplitude to $1\%$. When marginalizing over glitches or massive black hole binary transients, estimation errors remain flat up to transient signal-to-noise ratios of several hundred, whereas ignoring them severely biases likelihood fits. Under time-varying spline noise levels, realistic glitch rates, and gaps up to one day long, posterior coverage remains nominal or conservative across $\sim 10^4$ simulations. We test coverage in the local neighborhood of a given observation by introducing a novel importance-weighted localized simulation-based calibration test. We find flow matching slightly better calibrated than diffusion in simpler regimes and observe modest gains from physics-aware template inputs. Finally, we outline how these networks can initialize the noise and stochastic blocks of a LISA global fit.

cross.title: Ohmic warm inflation
cross.summary: We show that Warm Little Inflation is anomalous, lacks a suitable inflaton potential, and cannot sustain the thermal bath, as the quasi-static approximation over-estimated the dissipated power. To address these issues, we propose a new friction mechanism and new anomaly-free models based on one fermion charged under a U(1) gauge group in one extra dimension. The four-dimensional lattice version is a ring of $N$ U(1) groups with one fermion at each site, reducing to an anomaly-free version of the warm little inflaton model for $N=2$. The inflaton is a Wilson line, protected for $N\ge5$. Large $N$ allows a suitable monodromy inflaton potential. In the continuum limit, $N\to\infty$, the inflaton velocity becomes a five-dimensional electric field and friction becomes Ohmic dissipation, which seems able to sustain warm inflation compatibly with observations.

repl.title: Alleviating the Hubble tension with self-interacting ultralight dark matter
repl.summary: We study the possibility that a self-interacting ultralight dark matter field with a characteristic energy scale $\tilde{m}\simeq 1~{\rm eV}$ can behave like an extra radiation component before recombination. This additional radiation can reduce the sound horizon of the photon-baryon fluid. A smaller sound horizon can give a higher inferred value of the present-day Hubble parameter at the background level, and thus may help reduce the Hubble tension. This effect can be obtained without adding another dark sector component besides self-interacting ULDM. A full perturbation and likelihood analysis is needed to see if the model is consistent with CMB and structure-formation data.

repl.title: Scaling Relations for Dark Matter Halos Hosting Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxies
repl.summary: We consider the extraction of parameters of dark matter halos hosting ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, in the case where there are only ${\cal O}(10)$ identified member stars with measured line-of-sight velocities. This scenario is likely to be increasingly common, as upcoming newly discovered dwarf galaxies in the Milky Way, by e.g. the Rubin Observatory, will likely (at least initially) have only a few identified members. Assuming an NFW dark matter profile, equilibrium modeling likely can only robustly extract one halo parameter ($\rho_s r_s$), but the scale radius itself will typically be unconstrained. In these cases, the results obtainable from Jeans modeling can be well replicated by a simple scaling relation motivated by the half-light mass estimator. As a application, we examine the recently discovered stellar system Ursa Major III, which has been optimistically assessed to have the largest $J$-factor of any known object. We suggest that, because of the presence of outlier stars, the $J$-factor obtained from modeling of Ursa Major III is likely inflated, as it is inconsistent with the half-light mass estimator, while removal of the outliers will leave the $J$-factor unconstrained from below.

repl.title: Jet launching from the Kerr black hole magnetosphere: An electrogeodesic approach
repl.summary: The launch of relativistic jets of plasma on astrophysical to cosmological scales is observed in a variety of astrophysical sources, from active galactic nuclei to X-ray binaries. While these jets can be reproduced by general relativistic magneto-hydrodynamics (GRMHD) and particle-in-cells (GRPIC) simulations of the dynamical Kerr magnetosphere, the development of analytic models to describe the physics of the jets has remained limited. A key challenge is to analytically describe the individual trajectories of accelerated charged particles, which ultimately build up the jet and emit radiation. In this work, we provide a first simple but fully analytical model of jet launching from the Kerr magnetosphere based on the motion of charged particles. To that end, we use the integrability of electrogeodesic motion in the Kerr monopole magnetosphere to study the ejection of charged particles near the poles. This enables us to derive (i) a criterion for the rotation axis to constitute a stable latitudinal equilibrium position, thereby representing an idealized jet, (ii) the expression for the magnetic frame-dragging effect, and (iii) the condition for an asymptotic observer to measure blueshifted particles emanating from the black hole surroundings. Our study reveals that particles can be accelerated only in a specific region whose maximal radius depends on the spin and magnetization of the black hole. We further show that these results extend to the split-monopole Kerr solution by a redefinition of the angular momentum of the charged particles. Alongside these results, we provide a detailed review of the construction of test magnetospheres from (explicit and hidden) symmetries of the Kerr geometry and the condition for the separability of the electrogeodesic motion in a test magnetosphere, which serves as a basis for the model studied in this work.

repl.title: Dark Energy Survey Year 6 Results: Cosmological Constraints from Galaxy Clustering and Weak Lensing
repl.summary: We present cosmology results combining galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing measured in the full six years (Y6) of observations by the Dark Energy Survey (DES) covering $\sim$5000 deg$^2$. We perform a large-scale structure analysis using three two-point correlation functions (3$\times$2pt): (i) cosmic shear from 140 million source galaxy shapes, (ii) galaxy clustering of 9 million lens galaxy positions, and (iii) galaxy-galaxy lensing from their cross-correlation. We model the data in flat $\Lambda$CDM and $w$CDM cosmologies. The combined analysis yields $S_8\equiv \sigma_8 (\Omega_{\rm m}/0.3)^{0.5} = 0.789^{+0.012}_{-0.012}$ and matter density $\Omega_{\rm m} = 0.333^{+0.023}_{-0.028}$ in $\Lambda$CDM (68\% CL), where $\sigma_8$ is the clustering amplitude. These constraints show a (full-space) parameter difference of 1.8$\sigma$ from a combination of cosmic microwave background (CMB) primary anisotropy datasets from Planck 2018, ACT-DR6, and SPT-3G DR1. Projected only into $S_8$ the difference is $2.6\sigma$. In $w$CDM the Y6 3$\times$2pt results yield $S_8 = 0.782^{+0.021}_{-0.020}$, $\Omega_{\rm m} = 0.325^{+0.032}_{-0.035}$, and dark energy equation-of-state parameter $w = -1.12^{+0.26}_{-0.20}$. For the first time, we combine all DES dark-energy probes: 3$\times$2pt, SNe Ia, BAO and Clusters. In $\Lambda$CDM this combination yields a $2.8\sigma$ parameter difference from the CMB. When combining DES 3$\times$2pt with other low-redshift datasets (DESI DR2 BAO, DES SNe Ia, SPT clusters), we find a 2.3$\sigma$ parameter difference with CMB. A joint fit of Y6 3$\times$2pt, CMB, and those low-redshift datasets produces the tightest $\Lambda$CDM constraints to date: $S_8 = 0.806^{+0.006}_{-0.007}$, $\Omega_{\rm m} = 0.302^{+0.003}_{-0.003}$, $h = 0.683^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$, and $\sum m_\nu < 0.14$ eV (95\% CL). In $w$CDM, this combination yields $w = -0.981^{+0.021}_{-0.022}$.

repl.title: Interpreting the HI 21-cm cosmology maps through Largest Cluster Statistics III: Impact of the lightcone effect
repl.summary: The redshifted 21-cm signal emitted by neutral Hydrogen (HI) is a promising probe to understand the evolution of the topology of ionized regions during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). The topology of ionized regions allows us to infer the nature and properties of ionizing sources, i.e., early galaxies and AGNs. Traditional Fourier statistics, such as the power spectrum, help us quantify the strength of fluctuations in this field at different length scales but do not preserve its phase information. Analyzing the 21-cm brightness temperature field in the image domain retains its non-Gaussian characteristics and morphological information. One such approach is to track the coalescence of multiple ionized regions to form one contiguous ionized region spanning the universe. This is referred to as percolation, and its onset is quantified by a sharp rise in the value of the Largest Cluster Statistic (LCS) approaching unity. In this work, we carry out a percolation analysis of 21-cm brightness temperature maps by studying the redshift evolution of the LCS along a lightcone to distinguish between several simulated reionization scenarios. We estimate the LCS of subvolumes of different sizes in mock SKA-Low 21-cm lightcone maps and study their redshift evolution for different reionization scenarios using a moving volume approach. We find that the optimal size of the moving volume that reproduces the percolation transition from coeval maps varies across reionization scenarios and the evolution of LCS remains distinct across the reionization scenarios for a fixed moving volume bandwidth. The inferred percolation transition strongly depends on the synthesized beam width and the percentage gain calibration error, and is tractable for an optimistic SKA-Low observational setup.

repl.title: Successful irradiation campaign on PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA)/PRIMAger Kinetic Inductance Detectors with the Detector irRAdiation Cryogenic faciLity for Astrophysics (DRACuLA)
repl.summary: DRACuLA (Detector irRAdiation Cryogenic faciLity for Astrophysics) is a mobile dilution refrigerator platform developed at the Institut d'Astrophysique Spatiale (IAS) to expose sub-Kelvin detectors to particle beams at their nominal operating temperature, in the range 50 - 300 mK. We report on its design, beam-line integration at the Particle Therapy Research Center (PARTREC) in Groningen, and the operational performance achieved during the September 2025 irradiation campaign on Kinetic Inductance Detector (KID) arrays developed by SRON for the PRIMA mission. The detector samples were maintained at 120 mK throughout a 12-hour proton irradiation run at 184 MeV. The scientific results of this campaign are reported in a companion paper.

repl.title: Millimeter-wave Detections of Symbiotic Stars in SPT and ACT Data
repl.summary: We present the results of a joint targeted search of candidate symbiotic stars at millimeter wavelengths using the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT). Candidates are selected from the New Online Database of Symbiotic Variables, restricting to objects that are within either the SPT-3G or ACT~DR6 footprint, covering most of the southern hemisphere and up to a declination of $+20^\circ$. Forced photometry on the 828 candidate symbiotic star locations in SPT and ACT data results in 31 unique objects detected with more than a $3\sigma$ significance using two frequency bands: 18 confirmed and 13 suspected symbiotic stars. We provide the SPT and ACT 95/98, 150, and 220~GHz light curves, along with optical and infrared light curves from 2016--2026, as well as spectral energy distributions, physical parameters from the literature, and brief summaries regarding the nature of each individual object. Using Herschel SPIRE data from 2013, we place upper limits on millimeter flux for CN Cha near the beginning of the optical rise in its 2012/2013 nova, which suggests a strong variability and lag at millimeter wavelengths and results in a rare observance of a Galactic millimeter slow transient. In addition, we provide coadded thumbnails and light curves for the remaining 797 candidate symbiotic stars that did not pass our detection thresholds. Millimeter-wave emission from symbiotic stars is primarily a combination of free-free emission of the ionization region and optically thick blackbody emission of the cooler dust components of the system. When combined with contemporaneous multi-wavelength observations, millimeter-wave observations can be used to test binary models of symbiotic stars and provide insight on the geometry and physical properties of these systems.

repl.title: The 2MIG isolated AGNs. 3. Optical--IR variability and dust reverberation in the NLSy1 galaxies Mrk~42 and Mrk~493
repl.summary: We investigate optical and mid-infrared variability in two isolated narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, Mrk 42 and Mrk 493, using ZTF and WISE/NEOWISE light curves supplemented by ATLAS, SDSS, Swift, and IAC80 data. We examine colour-magnitude and flux-flux relations and measure optical-to-infrared lags with interpolated cross-correlation functions and flux-randomisation/random-subset-selection (FR/RSS), after correcting WISE fluxes for variable accretion-disc emission. For Mrk 42, the observed-frame W1 and W2 lags are 54 (+13/-33) and 62 (+7/-35) d, corresponding to redshift- and wavelength-corrected dust-response radii of 0.045 (+0.011/-0.028) and 0.052 (+0.006/-0.029) pc. For Mrk 493, the lags are 94 (+18/-21) and 111 (+26/-24) d, yielding radii of 0.078 (+0.015/-0.017) and 0.092 (+0.021/-0.020) pc. Both galaxies become optically bluer when brighter, but their W1-W2 colour responses differ: a significant relation is found in Mrk 493, whereas host and circumnuclear dilution may weaken it in Mrk 42. SDSS spectral decomposition provides a host-corrected AGN luminosity for comparison with the broad-line region in Mrk 42. The dust radii are consistent with the low-luminosity extension and scatter of published dust-radius--bolometric-luminosity relations. Mrk 42 also exhibits four broad maxima within a major optical flare, with a characteristic 45-47 d timescale; non-uniform peak intervals and stochastic-model tests favour substructure in a larger accretion-driven event. The results support disc-to-hot-dust reverberation in both galaxies while revealing distinct colour and optical-variability behaviour.

repl.title: Inpainting to search for premerger massive black hole binaries in realistic LISA datasets
repl.summary: A key science target of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is to carry out multi-messenger observations of massive black hole binaries, observing the merger simultaneously in gravitational waves and with electromagnetic observatories. Identifying that a merger is happening and providing an updating estimate of the sky location in the hours, days and weeks before the merger is critical to enable electromagnetic observations of the merger event. In this work we demonstrate and compare two methods for premerger identification of massive black hole binaries; a zero-latency filter approach and, for the first time, an approach using an ``inpainting'' technique. We apply these methods to the LISA Data Challenge dataset 2a--Sangria-HM--and demonstrate the successful recovery of the 14 signals in the dataset that we expected to be identifiable at least half a day before merger. We show that the inpainting method can identify premerger signals even when gaps are present in the data, demonstrating the recovery of a signal even when 3 day-long data gaps are added to the 14 days preceding merger. Finally, we explore the challenge of overlapping signals, using a region of overlapping signals in the Sangria-HM dataset, all of which merge within a 10-day window, and show how removing signals that have been confidently identified from the data allows us to identify quieter signals in the same period.

repl.title: The Radio-FIR Correlation in the Context of Deep Radio Source Counts
repl.summary: Increasingly deep, confusion-limited radio surveys have pushed direct radio source-count measurements down to tens of $\mu$Jy at 1.4 GHz. Confusion-noise P(D) analyses extend the statistical counts to below $1\,\mathrm{\mu Jy}$. Radio source counts have allowed for constraints on the radio-derived star formation rate density (SFRD) history through models of the backwards evolution of the local radio luminosity function, using the radio-FIR correlation, $q \propto \log(L_{\mathrm{FIR}}/L_{1.4})$, to convert radio luminosities to FIR luminosities and hence star-formation rates. Recent deep radio source counts from MeerKAT suggest a potential tension in the SFRD history between radio and UV/IR measurements at $1\lesssim z\lesssim 2$. This corresponds to a $\gtrsim 3\sigma$ discrepancy between the predicted and measured source counts near the star forming galaxy source count $S^2n(S)$ peak of ${\sim}30\,\mathrm{\mu Jy}$ under both a pure luminosity (PLE) and combined luminosity and density evolution (LADE). We consider what the requirement of agreement between radio source counts and the observed UV/IR SFRD indicates about the redshift evolution of the radio-FIR correlation and its intrinsic scatter out to $z=3$. We introduce a radio-luminosity based parameterization to $q_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)$ based on changing thermal radio fractions alone that agrees with the observed stellar-mass dependent $q_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)$ better than a non-evolving or decreasing $q_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)$. Despite this, we find that a decreasing $q_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)$ at fixed radio luminosity provides better agreement between source counts and the observed SFRD, while a $q_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)$ that breaks down due to cosmic ray losses requires an intrinsic scatter up to $\sigma_q\approx 0.3\,\mathrm{dex}$.

repl.title: Refined anti-proton and anti-deuteron fluxes from weak-scale Dark Matter
repl.summary: We provide the cosmic-ray (CR) fluxes of antiprotons and antideuterons produced by the Galactic annihilation or decay of weak-scale dark matter (DM) particles of masses in the range from a few GeV to 100 TeV. We estimate these fluxes based on the updated models for the propagation of charged particles in the Galaxy and using the improved $\bar{p}$ and $\bar{d}$ spectra provided by $\texttt{CosmiXs}$. For the updated propagation models we consider the MIN/MED/MAX sets under the new SLIM/BIG/QUAINT schemes. We treat the Galactic propagation in a semi-analytic way including different possible effects such as spatial diffusion, energy-losses, convection and diffusive reacceleration. For the DM distribution in the Galactic halo we consider NFW, Einasto and Burkert profiles with the most updated parameters. Moreover, we also incorporate the latest models for the inelastic cross-sections of $\bar{p}$ and $\bar{d}$ based on ALICE data. We validate our calculations with those available in the literature or those obtained from other publicly available numerical packages. We compare the CR fluxes obtained in this work with those provided previously by $\texttt{PPPC4DMID}$ which were based on old propagation scenarios. We find that the CR fluxes obtained here with the new propagation models are much more robust (compared to the older ones) under the variation MIN - MAX. We also discuss the impact of this in the improvement of the discovery potential of a possible DM signal in the light of the present and upcoming CR observations. We provide all our results for the DM-induced interstellar CR fluxes in a tabulated format (for the kinetic energy range 0.1 GeV - 100 TeV) in the $\texttt{GitHub}$ repository of the newly created $\texttt{CosmiXsPPPC}$ project. The results are ready to be used for studies related to DM indirect searches.

repl.title: Investigating black hole accretion and feedback self-regulation in Seyfert galaxies using the FIRE-3 cosmological hydrodynamic simulations
repl.summary: Observations of local Seyfert galaxies show an intriguing connection between AGN luminosity and a deficit of molecular gas on ~50pc scales compared to 200pc, the plausible imprint of AGN feedback. Motivated by these findings, we investigate the interplay between supermassive black hole (BH) accretion, AGN feedback, and nuclear gas reservoirs using cosmological hydrodynamic simulations implementing FIRE-3 multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) physics and multi-component BH accretion and feedback models. Focusing on the late-time evolution of four Milky Way-mass galaxies, we find recurrent cycles of increased gas inflow toward the accretion disc, enhanced BH accretion, feedback self-regulation, and suppressed gas inflow rate until the next fueling event. AGN winds interact with the ISM and escape preferentially through low-density polar channels after opening central cavities on ~10-500pc scales, regulating BH growth and producing episodic behaviour on ~10-100Myr timescales. The simulations reproduce the observed diversity of nuclear morphologies, gas concentrations, and AGN luminosities in late-type Seyfert galaxies, but do not exhibit a clear anti-correlation between gas concentration and AGN luminosity. Higher-luminosity AGN ($L_X$~$10^{41.5-43}$ erg s$^{-1}$) powered by the accretion disc reservoir can coexist with feedback-driven cavities, consistent with observations, but they are more common in simulated galaxies with centrally-peaked gas distributions. Although differences in sample selection, tracer choice, spatial resolution, and stochasticity in AGN fuelling may impact underlying concentration-luminosity trends, the apparent tension between simulations and observations points to the timing between gas inflow, accretion-disc depletion, and feedback-driven clearing on ~50-200pc scales as a key constraint on AGN self-regulation models.

repl.title: CARMApy: An Open-Source Python Framework for Simulating Microphysical Clouds in Planetary Atmospheres
repl.summary: CARMApy is a new open-source python code that performs bin-scheme microphysical modeling of clouds in exoplanet atmospheres. It models key cloud properties such as particle size distributions and microphysical rates from first principles. The code is a wrapper of ExoCARMA, a well tested Fortran code with an almost half century long heritage. CARMApy includes the microphysical processes of homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation, condensational growth, evaporation, coagulation, and vertical transport. CARMApy has 10 built-in default condensates and allows the user to specify additional condensates. In this work we describe CARMApy and the data products that it can generate, along with the history of its code heritage. We additionally compile a complete description of the theory and methods used in CARMA. Lastly we benchmark CARMApy and show that its results are consistent with previous versions of CARMA, while executing the code ~1.9 times faster single threaded ~3.8 times faster multithreaded.

repl.title: Probabilistic redshift estimation of undetected galaxies from multi-band background light maps
repl.summary: Accurate knowledge of the redshift distributions of undetected galaxy populations is essential for extracting the cosmological information encoded in the cosmic optical background. We present the first framework for estimating these distributions directly from multi-band maps of unresolved background light, using conditional normalising flows trained on realistic image simulations. For imaging quality comparable to that expected from the Euclid survey and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), our model achieves sub-per cent accuracy in both the mean and standard deviation of the flux-weighted redshift distributions when the training and target samples are statistically well matched. Furthermore, the network proves highly resilient to incomplete photometric coverage when combined with tailored data imputation strategies. To address the challenge of statistical mismatches between simulations and real observations, we propose incorporating observational quantities into the target variables, providing a built-in diagnostic to assess model reliability and uncertainty from the predictions themselves. We also demonstrate the feasibility of map-based tomographic analyses, showing that the model retains sufficient pixel-level detail to recover redshift distributions for tomographically defined subsamples with near sub-per cent accuracy across all bins.

repl.title: Sulfur photochemistry traces mantle redox states of rocky planets
repl.summary: Volatile outgassing from planetary interiors controls the composition of rocky exoplanets' secondary atmospheres. However, observations indicate that disequilibrium processes can strongly alter the chemical structure of hot Jupiters. How outgassing and photochemistry jointly determine the resulting atmospheric composition remains an open question. Sulfur-bearing species are promising tracers of interior-atmosphere coupling because their atmospheric abundances are sensitive to both mantle redox state and stellar irradiation. We investigate how photochemistry modifies outgassed atmospheres of diverse Earth-sized worlds during the magma ocean phase and assess how sulfur traces the interior oxidation state. The PROTEUS planetary interior-atmosphere evolution modelling framework is coupled to two chemical models, FastChem and VULCAN. We ran a grid of planetary evolution simulations spanning diverse mantle redox states, instellation fluxes, and host-star spectra. For each case, we compared atmospheric compositions with three post-processing calculations: thermochemical equilibrium, with disequilibrium vertical transport and with vertical transport plus photochemistry. The bulk atmospheric composition remains controlled by the mantle redox state and the history of outgassing. Reduced mantles produce atmospheres rich in H2 and CH4 and oxidised mantles are dominated by CO2 and H2O. Photochemistry affects the low-pressure upper atmosphere, strongly depleting neutral volatiles and enhancing radicals. Synthetic emission spectra show that photochemical SO2 can generate absorption features at 4 um and at 7.3/8.7 um, reaching ~60 ppm and ~100 ppm, respectively, before sequentially returning to the outgassed signatures of ~30 ppm and ~50 ppm for the oxidised mantle redox state. These signatures are potentially detectable with JWST, motivating targeted observational campaigns.

repl.title: Shape wall: Constraints on late-time solutions to the Hubble tension from the dimensionless expansion rate
repl.summary: The standard "no-go theorem" against late-time solutions to the Hubble tension is essentially a normalization wall, since Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements constrain the product $H_0r_d$, with $r_d$ the sound horizon at baryon drag. However, late-time solutions (which keep $r_d$ fixed) are tightly constrained not only by the BAO normalization $H_0r_d$, but also by the shape of the expansion history, i.e. the dimensionless expansion rate $E(z) \equiv H(z)/H_0$. We show that, if $r_d$ and the acoustic angular scale $\theta_s$ are fixed, an increase in $H_0$ needs to be matched by an equal fractional increase in the dimensionless distance integral $I \equiv \int dz/E(z)$: $\delta H_0/H_0 \simeq \delta I/I$. We use this to quantify the "shape wall" set by relative distance constraints on $E(z)$, which we reconstruct nonparametrically, using Gaussian Processes and the latest unanchored Type Ia Supernovae (SNeIa) and BAO data. In our most conservative analysis using PantheonPlus SNeIa and DESI DR2 BAO data, we find a maximum fractional increase in $H_0$ of $\lesssim 2\%$, falling well short of the $\gtrsim 8\%$ required to solve the tension. This shape wall holds even in the presence of early-time new physics, and limits the maximum increase in $H_0$ which can be contributed by late-time modifications to $E(z)$ at fixed $\theta_s$. Therefore, late-time modifications, whether invoked alone or alongside early-time new physics, face not only the well-known normalization wall, but also a stringent percent-level shape wall.

repl.title: Cataclysmic variables from Gaia XP spectra: The Gaia emission-line magnitude (GEM) diagram
repl.summary: Gaia DR3 opens a new window for the census of Galactic stellar populations in all-sky surveys, specifically for identifying cataclysmic variables (CVs). While the majority of CVs are distributed below the main sequence on the Gaia HR diagram, identifying them among dominant background stellar populations remains a significant challenge. Here, we present the Gaia Emission-line Magnitude (GEM) diagram - a tool designed to isolate CV candidates from background stars located below the main sequence. Using Gaia photometric data and low-resolution BP/RP (XP) spectra, we construct the GEM diagram by plotting the extinction-corrected absolute magnitude ($M_{G0}$) against the pseudo-equivalent width of the H$\alpha$ line ($pgEW_{H\alpha}$), which is computed via a Gaussian line-profile approximation. We find that known CVs and major stellar background populations, including white dwarfs, hot subdwarfs, and white dwarf-main sequence binaries, occupy distinct regions on the GEM diagram, reflecting both their physical properties and the low-resolution nature of the Gaia XP spectra. We define an empirical selection line on the GEM diagram to separate true H$\alpha$-emitting CVs from background contaminants. As a proof of concept, we apply the GEM diagram to a Gaia volume-limited sample within 250 pc ($G<17.5$ mag) distributed below the main sequence, recovering known CVs. Additionally, we identify three new CV candidates whose accreting nature is supported by archival X-ray data and optical variability. Compared to traditional optical color-based selection techniques, the GEM diagram uses Gaia's low-resolution spectra for initial target identification in all-sky surveys. This provides a more reliable framework for the statistical selection of CV candidates prior to ground-based spectroscopic follow-up and can be scaled to future Gaia data releases to map Galactic emission-line star populations.

repl.title: Locating the missing baryons in the warm-hot intergalactic medium with fast radio bursts and the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
repl.summary: Traditional astronomical censuses in the late-time Universe can only account for a fraction of the baryonic matter budget. Hydrodynamical simulations predict that the missing baryons reside in the vast filamentary structures of the cosmic web as a highly diffuse, warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM). Observing the WHIM directly has remained a long-standing challenge due to its typical temperature. In this study, we measure the angular cross-power spectrum between the dispersion measures (DMs) of fast radio bursts (FRBs) from the second CHIME/FRB catalog and the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) Compton-$y$ map from the Planck satellite. After masking cataloged galaxy clusters, we find a positive correlation between FRB DMs and the tSZ map at $>98\%$ confidence ($p_{\rm null}=0.0169$). With a temperature normalization of $2.4\times10^6\ {\rm K}$, we infer that a fraction $f_{\rm WHIM}=0.375^{+0.165}_{-0.161}$ of cosmic baryons resides in the hotter WHIM. These measurements constrain a substantial reservoir of hotter diffuse gas in the cosmic web and statistically close the cosmic baryon budget in the local Universe under the adopted density and pressure model.
